references.title: Video chapters
references.note: A chapter list starts at 00:00, has at least three timestamps in ascending order, and each chapter is at least 10 seconds; a manual list overrides automatic chapters.

references.title: Four tips to hook your viewers on YouTube
references.note: Anecdotal creator advice from 2014, with no data: open with a question, a branded flourish, a statement of what the video is, or a cold open.

references.title: Clickbait is Unreasonably Effective
references.note: One creator's uncontrolled anecdotes: clickable packaging can describe a video better than a plain topic label does.

references.authors: Jimmy Donaldson (MrBeast), as reproduced by Alexander Jarvis
references.title: MEMO: How to succeed in MrBeast production
references.note: A leaked internal memo that has not been authenticated; advice tuned to large-budget challenge entertainment, from internal analytics shown as screenshots.

references.authors: Alyce Currier, Ezra Fishman and Lisa Marinelli (Wistia)
references.title: Understanding Audience Retention
references.note: Vendor benchmarks with no disclosed sample or method: the first 2% of a video loses the most viewers.

references.title: Understanding In-Video Dropouts and Interaction Peaks in Online Lecture Videos
references.note: edX lecture videos from 2012 with autoplay: 36.6% of dropouts came in the first 3% of a video; 61% of sampled interaction peaks involved a visual transition.

references.authors: Philip J. Guo, Juho Kim and Rob Rubin
references.title: How Video Production Affects Student Engagement: An Empirical Study of MOOC Videos
references.note: Correlational MOOC data: median engagement at most 6 minutes whatever the length; tutorials watched 2 to 3 minutes; speaking rates from 48 to 254 wpm (mean 156).

references.authors: Derek A. Muller and Manjula D. Sharma
references.title: Tackling misconceptions in introductory physics using multimedia presentations
references.note: Abstract only: showing students common misconceptions in multimedia, even non-interactively, can help them overcome them; no effect sizes were available.

references.title: Online explainer videos: Features, benefits, and effects
references.note: A mini review of short explainers (one to three minutes): informal, voiced over, with a three-act structure described rather than tested.

references.title: Video abstract production guide
references.note: One team's account of one short science video: a script table with time, text and footage columns, planned at 150 spoken words per minute.

references.title: About our YouTube channel
references.note: A channel describing its own process: scripts take about a dozen drafts and the recorded narration times the animation; no outcome data.

references.authors: Selina A. Ruzi, Nicole M. Lee and Adrian A. Smith
references.title: Testing how different narrative perspectives achieve communication objectives and goals in online natural science videos
references.note: Randomised online experiment (515 participants, abstract-level reading): a scientist presenting their own work was rated more expert than a third-party presenter.

references.authors: Raphaela Martins Velho, Amanda Merian Freitas Mendes and Caio Lucidius Naberezny Azevedo
references.title: Communicating Science With YouTube Videos: How Nine Factors Relate to and Affect Video Views
references.note: Observational study of 441 Brazilian science videos: views per day were unrelated to video length (r = 0.005).

references.title: What Comprises a Successful Educational Science YouTube Video? A Five-Thousand User Survey on Viewing Behaviors and Self-Perceived Importance of Various Variables Controlled by Content Creators
references.note: Survey of more than 5,000 viewers of German science channels: stated preferences of self-selected fans, not measured behaviour.

references.title: Captioning Key: Presentation Rate
references.note: Caps educational captions at 130, 140 and 160 words per minute by level.

references.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.2.2: Captions (Prerecorded)
references.note: Level A: captions for prerecorded audio in synchronized media, including speaker identification and meaningful sounds; synthetic speech counts as audio.

references.title: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
references.note: Staff guidance for US law, not a legal opinion: disclose a brand relationship with the endorsement itself, in the video and not only the description.

references.title: Add branded content restrictions and disclosure labels
references.note: The paid promotion setting adds a label at the start of the video; creators remain responsible for applicable legal requirements.

references.title: Add end screens to videos
references.note: End screens fill the last 5 to 20 seconds, need a video of at least 25 seconds, and the help page advises leaving room in the last 20 seconds.

references.title: Set your channel or video's audience
references.note: Every creator must declare whether content is made for kids; YouTube may override the choice.

references.title: Fair use on YouTube
references.note: US fair use in four factors; credit, 'no infringement intended' and a disclaimer do not make a use fair; Content ID cannot decide fair use.
